title: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
summary: Split one smart-meter signal into per-appliance power: Hart's edge detection and ON/OFF matching, combinatorial optimisation and factorial HMMs, neural seq2point models, and how to score them.
outcomes: Explain why disaggregating one aggregate signal is ill-posed and what prior knowledge each method adds
Run Hart-style edge detection, clustering and ON/OFF matching by hand, and spot when simultaneous events break it
Compare combinatorial optimisation and factorial HMMs, including why their state space grows as K to the power N
Compute MAE, NEP, NDE, time-slice F1 and energy accuracy, and explain why they can disagree
Describe seq2point training windows and why evaluation on an unseen house matters

lessons.title: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem

blocks.md:
A smart meter reports one number per sample: the total power the home draws. **Energy disaggregation**, also called **non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM)**, estimates how that total splits across individual appliances, using only that single measurement point. *Non-intrusive* means nobody installs a sensor on each appliance; the alternative, **sub-metering**, puts a meter on every plug or circuit and is costly to install.

The motivating use case in the Neural NILM paper by Jack Kelly and William Knottenbelt is an itemised electricity bill produced from a single whole-home smart meter.

From the prerequisite courses you know how to treat a sampled signal and how to model a time series. NILM adds one twist: the signal you observe is a **sum of hidden signals**, and you must recover the parts.

Write $y^{(i)}_t$ for the power of appliance $i$ at sample $t$, $\bar{y}_t$ for the aggregate, and $\varepsilon_t$ for everything not modelled (noise, unknown loads):

blocks.caption: Real power adds, so the aggregate is a sum. At every sample you see one number and must infer N unknowns.

blocks.md:
One equation with $N$ unknowns per sample has infinitely many solutions, so the problem is **ill-posed**. Chaoyun Zhang and colleagues (seq2point, AAAI 2018) describe NILM as a single-channel blind source separation problem that is inherently unidentifiable. Every method in this course adds prior knowledge to pick one answer: appliance signatures, state models, or patterns learned from data.

We will use one toy house for the whole course: 60 samples, one per minute, with three appliances.

blocks.title: The toy house: when each appliance is on

scenes.caption: The fridge compressor cycles: on for 10 minutes, off for 10, three times (minutes 5-14, 25-34, 45-54). Each on period draws 120 W.
The kettle adds two short 2000 W spikes (minutes 18-20 and 40-41). It uses little time but a lot of energy.
A 60 W lamp is on from minute 10 to 44. Note minute 45: the lamp switches off in the same minute the fridge switches on. Keep an eye on it.

blocks.title: What the meter actually reports (watts per minute)

scenes.caption: The aggregate: the three appliances plus 0 to 10 W of simulated measurement noise. This is the only input a NILM algorithm gets.
The kettle minutes stand out at about 2060 W. Anything that shares those minutes (here the lamp) is hidden under a signal 30 times larger.
Levels near 120 W, 180 W and 60 W are fridge, fridge plus lamp, and lamp. From minute 45 the level is about 125 W again, but it is the fridge alone, not the lamp: the meter cannot tell you that.

blocks.md:
Two public datasets made NILM research comparable:

- **REDD** (J. Zico Kolter and Matthew Johnson, MIT, 2011) records whole-home current and voltage at 15 kHz, up to 24 labelled circuits at 0.5 Hz and up to 20 plug monitors at 1 Hz. The NILMTK paper calls it the first public dataset collected specifically for NILM; its public release has six houses.
- **UK-DALE** (Kelly and Knottenbelt, 2015) records five UK homes: whole-house signals at 16 kHz and individual appliances every 6 seconds. House 1 ran for 655 days with 54 channels.

Both give **ground truth**: sub-metered appliance signals recorded alongside the mains, so you can score an algorithm.

Real aggregates are not the clean sum of the appliances you know about. UK-DALE reports that in House 1, with monitors on almost every appliance, only 80% of the energy was sub-metered, partly because the 52 plug monitors themselves draw about 50 W. The $\varepsilon_t$ term is never zero.

NILM is an inverse problem: one observed sum, many hidden parts. Every algorithm you will meet differs only in what extra knowledge it uses to choose among the many decompositions that add up to the same total.

blocks.question: At minute 47 the meter reads 122 W. Which statement is correct using only that one reading?
options: It must be the fridge, because the fridge draws 120 W
It could be the fridge alone, or two 60 W lamps if the house had two, so one reading cannot decide
It must be the lamp plus 62 W of noise
It is the kettle in a low-power state
blocks.explain: A single reading only constrains the sum. With three known appliances, 120 W happens to match one combination, but adding a second 60 W lamp would create a second exact match. Context over time (what changed, and when) is what breaks such ties.

lessons.title: Hart's NALM: steady states, step changes and signatures

blocks.md:
George Hart, with Edward Kern and Fred Schweppe at MIT, designed the **Nonintrusive Appliance Load Monitor (NALM)** in the 1980s; their US patent 4858141 describes it, and Hart's 1992 *Proceedings of the IEEE* paper "Nonintrusive appliance load monitoring" describes it in depth. The NILMTK authors credit Hart with proposing the first algorithm for disaggregating household energy use.

The core idea, in the words of Hart's project page: if a refrigerator consumes 250 W and 200 VAR, a step increase of that size means it turned on, and a decrease of that size means it turned off.

The patent spells out a pipeline:

1. Measure real power $P$ and reactive power $Q$ at the meter and **normalise** them to a nominal voltage, so a voltage sag is not mistaken for an appliance event.
2. Detect **steady-state** periods: the patent's preferred tolerance is about 35 W or VAR over 2 seconds.
3. Record the **net change** $(\Delta P, \Delta Q)$ between consecutive steady states. These are the events, or edges.
4. **Cluster** the changes in the $\Delta P$-$\Delta Q$ plane; each tight cluster is one switching action of one appliance.
5. **Match** each positive cluster with a negative cluster of about equal and opposite size; each ON/OFF pair is one appliance.
6. Energy = power step x on-time. A lookup table names the appliance class.

blocks.caption: Voltage normalisation from Hart, as implemented in NILMTK. A resistive load's power scales with voltage squared, so this undoes voltage swings.

blocks.title: The event-based pipeline, stage by stage

scenes.caption: Raw voltage and current come in at the meter socket. Nothing is installed inside the home.
Normalisation removes the effect of supply voltage changes; edge detection waits for a steady level, then records the net step between steady levels.
Each step becomes a point (dP, dQ). Repeated switching of the same appliance produces a tight cluster of points.
A positive cluster is paired with a negative cluster of matching size. The time between paired ON and OFF events is the on-time.
Energy per appliance is step size times on-time, summed over all pairs. Simplified: Hart's later work adds multi-state appliance models.

blocks.md: Why measure reactive power at all? **Real power** $P$ (watts) does work; **reactive power** $Q$ (VAR) sloshes back and forth in motors and other inductive loads. A kettle or filament lamp is nearly resistive, so its $\Delta Q$ is near zero, while a fridge compressor motor has a large $\Delta Q$. Two appliances with the same wattage can sit far apart in the $\Delta P$-$\Delta Q$ plane. The patent's Figure 8 plots the clusters of changes exactly this way: real power on the x axis, reactive power on the y axis.

blocks.title: Same watts, different signature in the P-Q plane

scenes.caption: Hart's example fridge steps by 250 W and 200 VAR, so it sits on the line dQ = 0.8 dP.
A purely resistive 250 W load (hypothetical heater) has the same dP but lies on dQ = 0. In P alone the two would collide; in the P-Q plane they separate.

blocks.md: The method rests on what the NILM review by Klemenjak and Goldsborough calls Hart's **switch continuity principle**: in a short enough interval, the number of appliances changing state is small, ideally zero or one. That is what lets one observed step be read as one appliance's switching. The sample rate must be high enough to see steady periods between events.

Event-based methods need step changes. Hart's own NALM page lists three appliance classes: ON/OFF (bulbs, toasters), multi-state (washing machines, dishwashers with fill, rinse and spin states) and continuously variable (light dimmers, variable-speed tools). The last class is hard to monitor nonintrusively because it does not generate step changes in power.

blocks.question: A 1500 W kettle and a 1500 W space heater (both nearly resistive) live in the same house. Which feature from Hart's pipeline separates them best?
options: Nothing in a single (dP, dQ) step; you need other cues such as typical duration or time of day
Their reactive power steps, since dQ differs
Voltage normalisation, since it rescales each appliance differently
The steady-state tolerance of 35 W
blocks.explain: Both are resistive, so dQ is near zero for both and dP matches: the two points land in one cluster. Reactive power only helps when the loads differ in it. Normalisation is applied to the aggregate, not per appliance. Separating them needs extra features such as on-duration or usage patterns, which is why later models add temporal structure.

blocks.question: The supply voltage rises from 230 V to 240 V while every appliance stays on. What happens without voltage normalisation?
options: Nothing, power does not depend on voltage
The meter reports reactive power instead
Only the fridge is affected because it has a motor
Resistive loads draw more power, the aggregate steps up, and the edge detector may report a spurious event
blocks.explain: A resistive load draws power proportional to voltage squared, so every resistive appliance draws more and the total steps up with no appliance switching. Normalising to a nominal voltage removes that step, which is why Hart's pipeline normalises before edge detection.

lessons.title: Running edge detection and ON/OFF matching on the toy house

blocks.md:
Now apply a simplified version of Hart's pipeline to the toy aggregate. Our toy has only real power, one sample per minute, so the steps are:

1. **Edge detection**: take the first difference $\Delta_t = \bar{y}_t - \bar{y}_{t-1}$ and keep samples where $|\Delta_t| > 30$ W.
2. **Clustering**: group the edge magnitudes $|\Delta_t|$ with 1-D k-means, $k = 3$: repeatedly assign each value to the nearest of 3 centres, then move each centre to the mean of its values.
3. **Matching**: an ON edge opens an interval for its cluster; the next OFF edge of the same cluster closes it.
4. **Assignment**: each closed interval gets the cluster's mean step as its power.

scenes.caption: Each cell is the change from the previous minute. Noise moves the level by at most 10 W when no appliance switches.
Threshold |dP| > 30 W keeps 11 edges (green). The 30 W threshold sits between the 10 W noise and the smallest real step.

Two edges look odd. Minute 10 shows +51, not +60, because noise fell by 9 W in the same minute. Minute 45 shows +64: the lamp went off (-60) while the fridge came on (+120), so the meter sees only the net +64 (noise included).
The edges in time order. Signs say ON (+) or OFF (-); magnitudes say which appliance.
1-D k-means on |dP| converges to centroids 57.5, 118.8 and 2001.8 W. Naming the clusters lamp, fridge and kettle is the lookup-table step.
The +64 edge at minute 45 lands in the lamp cluster (|64 - 57.5| is smaller than |64 - 118.8|). The algorithm now believes the lamp switched ON at minute 45.

blocks.prompt: The lamp has been on since minute 10 (its +51 edge). Now a lamp ON edge arrives at 45 and a fridge OFF edge arrives at 55, but the fridge is not on according to the matcher. Predict the lamp and fridge estimates for minutes 45 to 59.
blocks.reveal: The lamp is already on, so the second ON edge is dropped. No lamp OFF edge ever arrives, so the lamp interval stays open to the end: **lamp estimated on for minutes 10 to 59**. The fridge OFF at 55 has no open ON, so it is dropped too: **fridge estimated off for minutes 45 to 54**. One collision causes two errors, 15 false-positive lamp minutes and 10 missed fridge minutes.

blocks.title: ON/OFF matching, edge by edge

scenes.caption: Edge detection keeps 11 of the 59 differences.
Clustering assigns each edge to lamp, fridge or kettle.
Minute 5, +121: fridge ON. The fridge interval opens.
Minute 15, -115: fridge OFF closes the interval (5, 15). Kettle pairs (18, 21) and (40, 42) and fridge (25, 35) follow the same way.
Minute 45, +64 labelled lamp, but the lamp is already on since minute 10. The edge is silently dropped.
Minute 55, -113: fridge OFF, but no fridge interval is open. Dropped again.
End of data: the lamp interval is still open, so it is closed at minute 60. Five pairs in total.

blocks.title: Ground truth versus the event-based estimate

scenes.caption: Estimates use the cluster centroids, rounded, as power: fridge 119 W, kettle 2002 W, lamp 58 W. The kettle is perfect in timing.
The errors all trace back to minute 45: the third fridge cycle is missed and the lamp never switches off. The kettle, whose edges never collide, is untouched.

blocks.md: Event-based NILM reads each step as one appliance switching. When two appliances switch inside one sample, the switch continuity assumption breaks: the net step looks like a third, unrelated appliance, and the ON/OFF bookkeeping fails for both. Higher sample rates make such coincidences rarer but never impossible.

blocks.question: Which change to the toy pipeline would most directly avoid the minute-45 failure?
options: Raise the edge threshold from 30 W to 70 W
Use more clusters in k-means
Sample faster so the lamp-off and fridge-on events fall in different samples
Use the cluster median instead of the mean as each appliance's power
blocks.explain: The failure comes from two events sharing one sample. Faster sampling separates them into two clean edges (-60 then +120). A 70 W threshold would drop the +64 edge but also the lamp's real +51 ON edge, and the fridge would still have no ON edge at 45. More clusters or a median do not undo a merged edge.

blocks.question: In this toy, which appliance would also be hurt if its ON edge merged with another event, given how the matcher is written?
options: Any appliance: a merged ON edge leaves that appliance's later OFF edge unmatched and dropped
None: only the lamp can be affected
Only the kettle, because its step is largest
Only appliances whose step is below the threshold
blocks.explain: The matcher drops an OFF edge whenever no ON is open for that cluster. Any appliance whose ON edge gets merged into a differently sized step loses that whole interval, exactly as the fridge did at minutes 45 to 54.

blocks.md:
Instead of reading edges, a second family of methods works on the **levels**. NILMTK ships two benchmark algorithms of this kind.

**Combinatorial optimisation (CO)**, which NILMTK attributes to Hart's 1992 paper, assumes each appliance has a few known power levels (learned from sub-metered training data). At each sample it picks the combination of appliance states whose summed power is closest to the aggregate:

blocks.caption: Each sample is solved on its own. With K states per appliance and N appliances there are K to the power N combinations to check.

blocks.title: CO on the toy: |aggregate minus combination| for six minutes

scenes.caption: Rows are minutes, columns the 8 on/off combinations of fridge (F), kettle (K) and lamp (L) with model powers 120, 2000 and 60 W. Each cell is the residual in watts.
CO picks the smallest residual in each row (highlighted). At minute 47, the fridge-only column wins with 2 W: CO gets the minute-45 collision right, because it never looks at edges.
Run over all 60 minutes, CO recovers every appliance exactly on this toy: MAE 0 W and F1 1.0 for all three. Simplified: the appliance models here are the true powers and the noise is tiny.

blocks.prompt: Add a 120 W television to the toy house. At minute 47 the reading is 122 W. What does CO do now?
blocks.reveal: Two combinations now sum to exactly 120 W: fridge alone and TV alone. Both have residual 2 W, so CO has a **tie** it cannot break; whichever it picks, it may be wrong for whole stretches. CO treats each sample independently, so it cannot use the fact that the level appeared together with a fridge-sized step at minute 45, or that the fridge was cycling every 20 minutes. The NILMTK paper also notes CO resembles the subset-sum problem and is NP-complete.

blocks.md:
The **factorial hidden Markov model (FHMM)** adds time. Each appliance is its own hidden Markov model: a hidden state (off, on, or several on-levels) that evolves with transition probabilities, and an emitted power for each state. The meter observes the sum of all emissions. Because states persist, a fridge that just turned on is likely still on next minute, which breaks ties CO cannot.

The price is size. An FHMM is equivalent to one big HMM whose state is the joint state of every appliance: $K^N$ joint states and a $K^N \times K^N$ transition matrix, so exact inference costs $O(T K^{2N})$.

blocks.title: A factorial HMM: independent chains, one summed observation

scenes.caption: Each appliance is its own Markov chain over time. Transition probabilities encode habits such as the fridge staying on for several minutes.
The observed aggregate at each time is the sum of the three emitted powers plus noise. Only these bottom nodes are seen.
Inference must decode all chains jointly. With two states each, the toy has 2^3 = 8 joint states; the transition matrix of the equivalent HMM has 64 entries.

blocks.title: How the joint state space explodes

scenes.caption: Two-state appliances: the toy's 3 appliances give 8 joint states; 20 appliances give about a million. NILMTK reports that the transition matrix for just 14 two-state appliances needs 8 GB of RAM.

REDD's FHMM baseline used 4 states per device and typically about 20 devices per home: 4^20, about 1.1 x 10^12 joint states. Kolter and Johnson therefore used blocked Gibbs sampling instead of exact inference.

blocks.md: Kolter and Tommi Jaakkola (AISTATS 2012) made FHMM inference practical with **AFAMAP** (additive factorial approximate MAP). It combines three ideas: model the **difference signal** $\bar{y}_t - \bar{y}_{t-1}$ as well as the total (Hart's edges reappear inside a probabilistic model), add a **robust mixture component** with an $\ell_1$ penalty that soaks up unmodelled loads, and constrain the posterior so **at most one chain changes state per time step**. The result is a convex quadratic program relaxation: no local optima, and cost that grows roughly linearly in the number of HMMs.

Do not read CO's perfect toy score as "CO beats event detection". CO was given the exact appliance powers and only three appliances with no sum collisions. Add one appliance whose power equals a sum of others, or real-world power that drifts, and per-sample matching breaks while temporal models degrade more gracefully.

blocks.question: Why does the one-change-per-step constraint in AFAMAP make sense for energy data?
options: Appliances are physically prevented from switching together
It forces the kettle to be modelled separately
It removes the need for training data
It restates the switch continuity principle: at short sample intervals, simultaneous switching is rare, and the constraint shrinks the search enormously
blocks.explain: Simultaneous switches are possible (our minute 45), but rare at short sampling intervals. Assuming at most one change per step turns an exponential joint search into one over N single-chain changes, which is what makes the convex relaxation efficient. It is a modelling assumption, so it will occasionally be wrong.

blocks.question: A house has 10 appliances with 3 states each. How many joint states does the equivalent single HMM have?
blocks.explain: Joint states are K to the power N = 3^10 = 59,049. 30 would be K times N (independent chains, which is what approximate methods exploit), 1,000 is 10^3 with base and exponent swapped, and 3,628,800 is 10 factorial.

lessons.title: Scoring a disaggregation: MAE, NEP, NDE and F1

blocks.md: The NILMTK paper (Nipun Batra, Jack Kelly, Oliver Parson and colleagues, 2014) points out a practical problem: papers on REDD used four slightly different accuracy metrics, so their numbers could not be compared. NILMTK fixed a common pipeline and a shared metric suite. The current NILMTK code defines, per appliance with truth $y_t$ and estimate $\hat{y}_t$ over $T$ samples:

blocks.caption: MAE is in watts. NEP (normalised error in assigned power) and NDE (normalised disaggregation error) are unitless, so appliances of different sizes can be compared.

blocks.md: For **F1**, NILMTK turns each sample into an on/off label with a 10 W threshold (below 10 W is off), then counts time slices: a **true positive** is a slice where the appliance is on and predicted on, a **false positive** is predicted on while off, a **false negative** is predicted off while on. Precision $= TP/(TP+FP)$, recall $= TP/(TP+FN)$, and F1 is their harmonic mean. Note that this F1 is about time slices, not about detecting switching events.

blocks.title: Minutes 40-59: where the event method's errors come from

scenes.caption: Truth and estimate side by side for the last 20 minutes, in watts.
Fridge: 10 false negatives (minutes 45-54), each off by 120 W. Earlier cycles were right except a 1 W offset (119 vs 120) on 20 minutes.
Lamp: 15 false positives (minutes 45-59), each off by 58 W, plus a 2 W offset on the 35 true minutes.

blocks.md: Working the fridge through by hand: absolute error is $20 \times 1 + 10 \times 120 = 1220$ W-minutes over 60 minutes, so MAE $= 20.33$ W. True fridge energy is $30 \times 120 = 3600$, so NEP $= 1220/3600 = 0.339$. Squared error is $20 + 10 \times 120^2 = 144{,}020$ against $\sum y^2 = 432{,}000$, so NDE $= \sqrt{0.3334} = 0.577$. With $TP = 20$, $FP = 0$, $FN = 10$: precision 1.0, recall 0.667, F1 0.8.

blocks.title: Event-based method on the toy, metric by metric

scenes.caption: MAE in watts: fridge 20.33, kettle 0.17, lamp 15.67. The kettle's only error is its 2 W offset on 5 minutes.
NEP: fridge 0.339, kettle 0.001, lamp 0.448. Normalising by each appliance's own energy shows the lamp is proportionally the worst.
NDE: fridge 0.577, kettle 0.001, lamp 0.634. Squaring punishes the large 120 W and 58 W misses more than the small offsets.
F1 on 10 W on/off labels: fridge 0.8 (recall 0.667), kettle 1.0, lamp 0.824 (precision 0.7). CO scores 1.0 on all three on this toy.

blocks.md: REDD's original paper scored the FHMM with **energy correctly assigned**, which sums errors over all appliances and divides by twice the aggregate energy (each misassigned watt is counted once as missing and once as extra):

blocks.caption: Kolter and Johnson's metric; Kelly and Knottenbelt use the same form as proportion of total energy correctly assigned.

blocks.prompt: The event method mislabels 25 appliance-minutes in the toy. Guess its energy-correctly-assigned score Acc.
blocks.reveal: Total absolute error is $1220 + 10 + 940 = 2170$ W-minutes, and the aggregate sums to 15,988 W-minutes, so $\text{Acc} = 1 - 2170/(2 \times 15988) = 0.932$. It looks excellent, because the kettle, with 10,000 of the 15,700 appliance W-minutes, is nearly perfect. An energy-weighted score can hide large errors on small appliances, which is why NILMTK reports several metrics per appliance.

blocks.title: Energy per appliance over the hour (Wh), truth versus estimate

scenes.caption: Truth: fridge 60 Wh, kettle 166.67 Wh, lamp 35 Wh (one sample per minute, so W-minutes divided by 60).

Estimate: fridge 39.67 Wh (one cycle missed), kettle 166.83 Wh, lamp 48.33 Wh (15 extra minutes). An itemised bill would under-report the fridge by about 20 Wh and over-report the lamp by about 13 Wh.

blocks.md: Metric details change numbers silently. The on/off threshold (10 W in NILMTK) sets F1; whether a paper reports NEP, NDE or energy accuracy changes which appliances look good; and per-appliance averages weight a lamp and a kettle equally while energy accuracy is dominated by the kettle. Always state the metric definition alongside a number.

blocks.question: Your model gets an energy-correctly-assigned score of 0.93 on a house. A user complains that the fridge estimate is badly wrong. Which is the most likely explanation?
options: The metric has a bug, since 0.93 rules out a large fridge error
The fridge must be below NILMTK's 10 W threshold
The metric is weighted by energy, so a well-estimated high-energy appliance can dominate while a smaller one is badly wrong
Energy accuracy only counts false positives
blocks.explain: Acc sums absolute errors over all appliances and divides by total energy. In the toy, Acc is 0.932 while the fridge NEP is 0.339 and the lamp NEP is 0.448. Look at per-appliance MAE, NEP or F1 to find such problems.

blocks.question: Two models have the same fridge MAE. Model A is off by 5 W on every sample; model B is exactly right except for a few samples off by a lot. Which metric separates them, and how?
options: NDE: B scores worse because squaring weights its few large errors more
F1: A scores lower because small offsets flip the on/off labels
NEP: A scores worse because it has more errors
None: equal MAE means every normalised metric is equal
blocks.explain: NEP is MAE times T divided by total energy, so equal MAE means equal NEP. NDE squares errors, so B's few large misses count more. F1 barely moves for A, since a 5 W offset on a 120 W fridge does not cross the 10 W on/off threshold.

lessons.title: Neural NILM, seq2point, and the unseen-house problem

blocks.md:
Kelly and Knottenbelt's **Neural NILM** (BuildSys 2015) trained one deep network per target appliance. The input is a window of aggregate power; the target is that appliance's power over the same window. They adapted three architectures: an LSTM, a denoising autoencoder, and a "rectangles" network that regresses the start time, end time and average power of an activation.

Window width was chosen per appliance, from 128 samples (13 minutes) for the kettle to 1536 samples (2.5 hours) for the dish washer, at UK-DALE's 6-second rate. Width matters: with a 1024-sample fridge window the autoencoder learned nothing useful, while 512 samples let it reach F1 0.87.

Two training ideas from that paper are worth keeping:

- **Synthetic aggregates.** Since appliances add, you can paste real sub-metered appliance activations into windows to fabricate unlimited aggregate data. Mixing synthetic and real data 50:50 acted as a regulariser and appeared to improve generalisation to unseen houses. Validation and testing used real data only.
- **Test on a house not seen in training.** On the unseen house, the autoencoder and rectangles nets beat NILMTK's CO and FHMM on every appliance on F1, precision, energy correctly assigned and MAE. The LSTM beat them on two-state appliances (kettle, fridge, microwave) but not on multi-state ones (dish washer, washing machine).

Sliding a sequence-to-sequence network along a long signal means each sample is predicted many times, once per window that covers it, and the overlapping predictions must be averaged. Zhang and colleagues' **sequence-to-point (seq2point)** instead maps a window of mains to a single value: the target appliance's power at the **midpoint** of the window. The reasoning: a midpoint sample has context on both sides, unlike samples near a window's edges.

blocks.caption: One output per window. The paper uses W = 599 samples for every appliance, with inputs and targets standardised (subtract mean, divide by standard deviation).

blocks.title: Seq2point training pairs on the toy (W = 9)

scenes.caption: A window of 9 mains samples centred on minute 45 (shaded) becomes one input; the fridge power at minute 45 (120 W) is its single target.

Slide by one: centred on 47 the window spans 43-51 and the target is fridge power at 47. Unlike the edge matcher, the window shows the level stayed near 125 W, the fridge's level, not the lamp's 60 W.
Centred on 52, the window already contains the drop to about 8 W at minute 55: future context informs the midpoint estimate.
Centred on 55 the target is 0 W. On a 60-sample series, W = 9 yields 60 - 9 + 1 = 52 training pairs, with midpoints 4 to 55; the first and last 4 minutes need padding to get predictions.

blocks.md: The seq2point network is a stack of five 1-D convolution layers (30, 30, 40, 50 and 50 filters of widths 10, 8, 6, 5 and 5, ReLU, stride 1), a 1024-unit dense layer and a single linear output. On UK-DALE they trained on houses 1, 3, 4 and 5 and tested on house 2; on REDD, trained on houses 2 to 6 and tested on house 1. Compared with Kelly's seq2seq autoencoder, seq2point reduced overall MAE by 84% and signal aggregate error (relative error in total energy) by 92% on UK-DALE. The authors also show the convolution filters respond to change points in the mains: the network learns Hart's edges on its own.

Every NILM method injects prior knowledge to resolve an unidentifiable sum. Hart hand-designs it (step signatures), FHMMs encode it as state machines, and neural nets learn it from sub-metered houses. The test that matters is a house the model never saw.

Open problems the sources keep returning to:

- **Multi-state and variable loads.** Washing machines and dishwashers cycle through states; dimmers and variable-speed drives produce no clean steps.
- **Unseen houses.** REDD's FHMM baseline scored 64.5% energy correctly assigned when trained and tested in the same houses but 47.7% on a held-out house (a simple mean predictor: 42.7% and 25.9%).
- **Unmetered loads.** Ground truth rarely covers the whole aggregate, as UK-DALE's 80% sub-metered house shows.
- **Privacy.** In 1989 Hart warned that the same technique could reveal what people do at home, and REDD's authors store no identifying information about the houses and release only historical data for that reason.

blocks.question: A seq2point model for the fridge is trained with W = 599 at 6-second samples. Which input does it use to predict fridge power at time t?
options: Only the mains sample at time t
About an hour of mains before time t only
About an hour of mains centred on time t, past and future
The fridge's own past power readings
blocks.explain: 599 samples x 6 s is about 60 minutes in total, roughly 30 minutes on each side of the midpoint. Seq2point is non-causal: it uses both past and future mains. It never sees sub-metered fridge data at test time, only the aggregate.

blocks.question: A model reaches F1 0.95 on houses it was trained on and 0.60 on a new house. What is the most useful next step suggested by this course's sources?
options: Report 0.95, since the training houses are representative
Shrink the window to one sample to avoid overfitting
Switch to CO, which needs no training data
Add synthetic aggregates built from activations of many houses and evaluate on a held-out house
blocks.explain: Kelly and Knottenbelt found that mixing synthetic aggregates with real data regularised the nets and helped on unseen houses, and both they and Zhang and colleagues test on a held-out house. A one-sample window throws away the context that makes neural NILM work, and CO still needs appliance models learned from sub-metered data.
